planting.note: Grow as a houseplant in bright, indirect light in well-drained potting mix; slower-growing and more compact than its sister species Howea forsteriana, with distinctively arching, curled fronds.

directions: Grow in bright, indirect light in well-drained potting mix, letting the top couple of inches dry between waterings. Native alongside Howea forsteriana on Australia's Lord Howe Island, this species carries stiffer, more upright fronds that arch and curl distinctly at the tips, giving it a denser, more compact silhouette than the flatter-leaved kentia palm. It grows even more slowly than its sister species, which keeps it manageable as a long-term container specimen but also makes larger plants more expensive and less commonly available in the trade. It shares the kentia palm's excellent tolerance of low indoor light and dry air, making it one of the most forgiving palms for interior spaces. Keep it away from cold drafts and temperatures below 50°F, and wipe the fronds occasionally to remove dust and discourage spider mites.
sources: Fairchild Tropical Botanic Garden palm collection records

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant in bright, indirect light in well-drained, fertile potting mix; prized for its fuzzy, rust-orange crownshaft that gives the species both of its common names.

directions: Grow in bright, indirect light with some tolerance for morning direct sun, in well-drained, fertile potting mix kept evenly moist. This Madagascar palm is named for its striking crownshaft, densely covered in fine, rust-orange to reddish-brown fuzz that looks sunburned from a distance and feels soft like a teddy bear up close, a texture unlike any other palm commonly grown indoors. It grows considerably faster than many other collector palms once established, tolerating brighter light and slightly drier conditions than the closely related golden cane palm. Feed regularly during the growing season with a palm-specific fertilizer to prevent the yellowing common in potassium-deficient container palms, and keep it above 40°F to avoid cold damage.
sources: Montgomery Botanical Center palm collection records

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant in bright, indirect light in consistently moist, well-drained potting mix; a much more compact relative of the common majesty palm, better suited to smaller rooms.

directions: Grow in bright, indirect light in consistently moist, well-drained potting mix, since this Madagascar riverbank native has little tolerance for drying out completely. Unlike the towering Ravenea rivularis sold widely as majesty palm, this dwarf relative stays a fraction of the size, making it a better fit for tabletop or smaller-room display without sacrificing the same feathery, dark green fronds. It shares the genus's reputation for being fussier indoors than tougher palms like kentia, showing quick browning if humidity drops too low or the soil dries out between waterings. Mist regularly or use a pebble tray to boost humidity, feed lightly during the growing season, and keep it away from cold drafts and temperatures below 50°F.
sources: Kew Science, Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio specimen in bright, indirect light in rich, moisture-retentive, well-drained potting mix; larger and more robust than the smaller ruffled fan palm (Licuala grandis).

directions: Grow in bright, indirect light in rich, consistently moist, well-drained potting mix, since this Southeast Asian understory palm naturally grows along humid forest streambanks. Its huge, nearly circular, pleated fan leaves attach to the petiole at a central point, giving each frond a distinctive shield-like or peltate shape considerably larger and more dramatic than the smaller, more finely divided leaves of the popular ruffled fan palm. It needs consistently high humidity and steady warmth to thrive, showing brown leaf-edge scorch quickly in dry indoor air or cold drafts. Water generously and mist regularly, keep it well away from temperatures below 50°F, and site it where its bold, architectural foliage has room to fully expand.
sources: Kew Science, Plants of the World Online

common_name: Giant Mountain Fishtail Palm (Thai Giant Fishtail Palm)

planting.note: Plant in bright, filtered light in rich, well-drained soil in zone 10-12, or grow as a large container specimen indoors while young; unlike the clustering fishtail palms commonly sold as houseplants, this species grows as a single massive trunk.

directions: Plant in bright, filtered light in rich, well-drained, consistently moist soil, or grow young plants as a large container specimen indoors before eventual outdoor planting in frost-free climates. Native to the mountain forests of Thailand and neighboring regions, this is one of the largest fishtail palms in cultivation, developing a solitary gray trunk topped with an immense crown of drooping, doubly-compound fronds made up of ragged, fish-tail-shaped leaflets. Unlike the smaller, suckering clustered fishtail palm commonly sold as a houseplant, this species forms a single towering trunk and, like all Caryota, flowers from the top down and dies after its lowest inflorescence finishes fruiting. Provide steady warmth, high humidity, and generous water for the fastest growth, and protect young plants from any frost, since mature height and cold tolerance develop only after many years.
sources: Kew Science, Plants of the World Online
